The Dust Bowl

The Dust Bowl was a period of severe dust storms that greatly damaged the ecology and agriculture of the American and Canadian prairies during the 1930s. The phenomenon was caused by a combination of severe drought and a failure to apply dryland farming methods to prevent wind erosion of the soil.

During the previous decades, extensive deep plowing of the virgin topsoil of the Great Plains had displaced the native, deep-rooted grasses that normally trapped soil and moisture even during periods of drought and high winds. When the drought struck, the exposed soil turned to dust and blew away in enormous clouds that sometimes blackened the sky for days.

The storms reached as far as the East Coast, where dust settled on ships in the Atlantic Ocean and on the streets of New York and Washington. On April 14, 1935, a day remembered as Black Sunday, one of the worst storms swept across the southern plains and turned day into night.

The disaster forced tens of thousands of poverty-stricken families to abandon their farms. Many of these migrants, often called Okies regardless of the state they came from, traveled west to California in search of agricultural work, only to find that conditions there were little better than those they had left.

In response, the federal government created the Soil Conservation Service in 1935 and encouraged farmers to plant shelterbelts of trees, rotate crops, and plow along the contours of the land. These practices gradually reduced erosion, and the return of regular rainfall at the end of the decade brought the worst of the crisis to a close.
